claims.text: Prolonged thermal exposure within service-regime temperatures promotes nucleation and growth of intermetallic compounds from an initially metastable solid solution in Mg-containing lightweight HEAs.
Intermetallic precipitates formed along grain boundaries disrupt the continuity and adhesion of protective oxide films.
Disruption of protective oxide films by intermetallic precipitation reduces high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Intermetallic precipitation and associated oxide-film disruption reduce corrosion resistance.
Varying dwell time and ramp rate can induce controlled intermetallic precipitation in the proposed Mg-containing alloy.
Rapid quenching preserves the initial metastable solid-solution state.
The relevant structural mediator is the volume fraction and grain-boundary distribution of precipitated intermetallic phases.
Thermal exposure accelerates transformation from a metastable solid solution toward equilibrium intermetallic compounds.
Formation of intermetallic phases reduces microstructural homogeneity.
Intermetallic phase formation compromises the formation of a dense protective oxide scale.
Dense, continuous oxide or passive films improve oxidation and corrosion resistance.
Longer thermal dwells will increase the intermetallic phase fraction relative to the initial state.
Thermally exposed samples will develop a less continuous and less passivating surface oxide than rapidly quenched samples.
Thermally exposed samples will show worse oxidation and corrosion performance than rapidly quenched samples.
Rapidly quenched samples contain minimal intermetallic precipitation and have superior corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
The proposed effects apply around 900 °C and in aggressive environments such as 3.5 wt% NaCl solution.
Minor compositional changes can alter phase formation and corrosion or oxidation behavior in HEAs.
The transformation kinetics and quantitative performance impact in the proposed Mg-containing system remain undetermined.
